One way to open a glass jar with a metal lid is to run the lid under hot water.

Metal conducts heat much faster than glass, therefore the heat will spread across the lid before it has time to significantly heat up the glass.

With most solids, when you heat them up, they expand. And metals generally have a significantly higher coefficient of thermal expansion than glass.

The rate of expansion can be calculated with the formula

dl = L0 α (t1 - t0)

For instance steel has a thermal coefficient of 0.000012, a 75mm diameter steel lid that is heated from 15C (normal room temp) to 65C, will expand to 75.045mm.

Glass has a thermal coefficient of 0.0000059, heating a 75mm diameter glass jar from 15C to 65C will cause it to expand to 75.0221

So, not only will the metal lid expand more than the glass, since it conducts heat faster, it will expand faster.

If you can heat just the lid, you can temporarily make it 1/20th of a millimeter bigger, therefore a looser fit, and easier to turn. Just remember to use a towel so you don't burn your hands (because the metal conducts heat, to your hand).

I'm not referring to specific heat, that refers to the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of a given mass of a specific material.

I'm talking about conducting heat. i.e. If you heat up one end of a metal bar, how long does it take for the the whole bar to reach the same temperature? e.g. You can poke one end of a wooden stick in a fireplace and hold the other end without burning your hand, because wood has poor thermal conductivity. If you try the same thing with a metal rod, your hand will start getting rather hot, rather quickly.

In this particular instance, I'm talking about being able to heat up the entire metal lid quickly, and evenly. Glass has low thermal conductivity. So while part of the jar may be warmed up, the heat won't spread to the rest of the glass very quickly.

In physics, thermal conductivity (often denoted k, λ, or κ) is the property of a material to conduct heat. It is evaluated primarily in terms of Fourier's Law for heat conduction.
